stories.title_en: Japan's Hometown Tax (2018)

comments.author: cloudbonsai
comments.text:
This is a way weirder system than the name suggests. patio11 explains it in detail in the article, but the gist is:
1. You can contribute to rural areas in return for a tax credit, effectively allowing you to redirect a portion of your taxes to another town.
2. The most important quirk of the system is that you can choose
any towns
to contribute to. There is no requirement of previous residence or whatever. In fact, most people contribute to towns with which they have no personal connection.
3. This ended up causing tax competition among local governments. Quite a few towns started advertising expensive "gifts" to contributers ("Give us your taxes and we'll send you some goodies"). It went so far that some towns got banned from the hometwon tax system.
It was introduced with good intension, but resulted in a very inefficient tax system.

- Allow the developer to specify the common location(s) that they need access to. comments.author: smj-edison
comments.text: Reading this, it seems they're using the term "geometry" in a more abstract sense. Pretty much you can turn a reaction's state into an abstract point, and then you can plot that reaction point over time. It becomes concrete again when they plot the path of the reaction's "coordinates" and you can visually see what happened with the reaction. It's quite elegant! Like you can see a system oscillate if it circles forever, or you can see it converge if it spirals inwards.

Arithmetic can be "actually geometry" if you're good with a compass and straight edge and the use of geometry to understand numbers is old.

MCP servers to me seems like a dead man walking technology and I don't understand the point of it.
It adds security but...

- adds another system that requires maintenance and securing to prevent compromise.
- takes machine resources
- duplicates a subset of what can easily be harness functionality
- duplicates services and security (usually) of existing APIs, or adds another layer on top.
Whereas ultimately an AI harness
- will improve and optimise its own skills performing the same MCP functions
- can use plugins
- can have harness centralised (common) security controls and behaviours

stories.title_en: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is cable, AT&T says in false advertising case

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text:
Fiber is so much better than cable in an emergency. The equipment consumes significantly less power and is likely to stay up longer during a power outage. You get way more customers on each battery / generator.
I had an FTTH provider with 100% of their network on natural gas standby generators. Went through a week long power outage without losing a single packet. You can support something like 100k households with well under 50kW of power. There are homes with larger generators than this. Docsis 4 would put you somewhere around half a megawatt.

comments.author: userbinator
comments.text:
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds.
You can get symmetric DOCSIS, and apparently Comcast do offer that service[1]. Likewise, FTTH can be asymmetric if they set the traffic shaping that way. IMHO the only things that matter to the average user about an Internet connection are bandwidth, volume, and availability. As long as it terminates in WiFi or a standard Ethernet connector and passes IP traffic at the rate I paid for, I personally don't care what the physical infrastructure beyond the demarc is.
In fact, anecdotes from a few people I know have been that service interruptions actually
increased
after they upgraded to FTTH from DOCSIS.

No big surprises here. Big outages at big firms seem to always look like this.
The electricity industry has this notion they call a black start, where they bring the grid online from zero. It's a very difficult operation because you can't start a generator straight into an offline grid otherwise it gets hit with full demand and can't keep frequency in the right range, which can damage equipment. So they have to start by disconnecting all the loads and then bringing load blocks back in sequence, trying to roughly balance available generation with the size of the next block. In practice black starts are extremely rare, but they can happen after a cascading failure in which something causes some generating stations to trip, redirecting load onto the remaining stations which can't handle it causing them to trip in turn. The entire grid can collapse in just 60 seconds or so once that kind of runaway failure starts.
